content: These reactions can range from mild skin irritation to severe, life-threatening anaphylaxis. Latex is derived from the sap of the Hevea brasiliensis tree and contains proteins that can provoke immune responses in susceptible individuals. The allergy is categorized into three main types of reactions: Type I hypersensitivity, Type IV hypersensitivity, and irritant contact dermatitis. Type I Hypersensitivity Type I hypersensitivity is an immediate and potentially severe allergic reaction caused by IgE-mediated immune responses to latex proteins. Mild symptoms include skin redness, hives, and itching, while more severe reactions involve respiratory issues such as sneezing, nasal congestion, itchy eyes, asthma, and, in rare cases, anaphylactic shock. This type of reaction is particularly concerning in perioperative settings, especially for children with myelomeningocele, who are at higher risk. Type IV Hypersensitivity Type IV hypersensitivity, also known as allergic contact dermatitis, is a delayed reaction caused by chemicals added during the processing of latex. This type of reaction is not mediated by latex proteins but rather by the chemical additives used in manufacturing. Irritant Contact Dermatitis Irritant contact dermatitis is the most common reaction to latex and is not an allergic response. Symptoms include dry, itchy, and irritated skin, particularly on the hands. While not an allergy, this condition can increase the risk of developing a true latex allergy over time. Diagnosis of Latex Allergy Diagnosing latex allergy involves a thorough medical history, physical examination, and specific tests. Blood tests, such as the radioallergosorbent test (RAST), can detect latex-specific IgE antibodies. Skin prick tests are commonly used for allergen testing, but no FDA-approved reagents for latex skin testing are currently available in the United States. Patch testing can identify Type IV reactions caused by chemical additives. All testing should be conducted in medical facilities equipped to manage severe allergic reactions. Products Containing Latex Latex is found in a wide range of products, including medical supplies (e.g., gloves, catheters, syringes), personal protective equipment (e.g., masks, goggles), household items (e.g., balloons, rubber bands, dishwashing gloves), and industrial materials (e.g., tires, carpeting). Individuals with latex allergy should be vigilant about avoiding these products and seek latex-free alternatives. Populations at Risk Certain groups are at higher risk of developing latex allergy: Children with myelomeningocele or spina bifida: Healthcare workers: Between 4% and 17% of healthcare professionals, including nurses, physicians, and technicians, experience latex-related reactions due to frequent glove use. Industrial rubber workers: Individuals with multiple surgeries: Latex-Fruit Syndrome Some individuals with latex allergy also exhibit cross-reactivity to certain fruits and plant products, a condition known as latex-fruit syndrome. Commonly implicated foods include bananas, avocados, chestnuts, kiwis, and mangoes. In severe cases, even foods handled with latex gloves can provoke allergic reactions. Treatment and Management The cornerstone of managing latex allergy is strict avoidance of latex-containing products. For individuals with confirmed latex allergy, workplaces and healthcare facilities should implement latex-safe protocols. Medications such as antihistamines and corticosteroids may alleviate symptoms, but they do not prevent reactions. In cases of severe allergy, patients should carry epinephrine auto-injectors and wear medical alert bracelets. Case Reports Several case studies illustrate the severity of latex allergy: 1. A laboratory technician developed asthma symptoms from airborne latex particles after wearing latex gloves. 2. A medical supply inspector experienced occupational asthma due to inflating latex gloves coated with cornstarch. 3. 4. A midwife suffered anaphylactic shock during a routine examination involving latex gloves. 5. A physician experienced collapse and required resuscitation after wearing latex gloves. 6. An intensive care nurse endured multiple severe allergic reactions, culminating in an episode of anaphylactic shock. Recommendations for Prevention For Employers: Use powder-free, low-protein latex gloves if latex gloves are necessary. Implement rigorous housekeeping practices to minimize latex dust in the workplace. Educate workers about latex allergy and its prevention. Screen high-risk workers periodically for early signs of latex allergy. For Workers: Use non-latex gloves for non-infectious tasks. Avoid oil-based hand creams when wearing latex gloves, as they can degrade the gloves. Wash hands thoroughly after glove removal. Learn to recognize symptoms of latex allergy and seek medical evaluation if symptoms occur. Inform employers and healthcare providers about latex allergy and wear medical alert identification.
